name: Merck stitch otoplasty
lead: The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive ear-pinning (otoplasty) method in which permanent sutures are placed through small stab incisions in the groove behind the ear to pull prominent ears closer to the head, without cutting the cartilage. People choose it to bring protruding ears into proportion with a shorter, less invasive procedure than an open operation.[2]

W. H. Merck reportedly developed the technique in 1995, began using it on patients in 1996 and described it in a 2013 publication. He reports that it works without cartilage scoring or cutting and cites several thousand operated ears, though these claims are not independently verified in the source.[2] It falls within the suture-only group of otoplasty techniques and is contrasted with Mustarde's open approach, which exposes the cartilage and removes skin.[1]
No published clinical studies of the Merck stitch itself were found; its reported results rest largely on Merck's own description.[2]
infobox: W. H. Merck (reportedly 1995; used on patients from 1996) [2]

paras: The surgeon makes small stab incisions in the groove behind the ear. Permanent, non-absorbable sutures are placed under the skin around the antihelix cartilage, tightened and knotted, which draws the ear closer to the head. The cartilage is not cut or reshaped. A protruding earlobe can also be pinned back if the cartilage extends into it.[2]

Wikipedia contrasts this with Mustarde's open method, in which the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, some skin is removed and mattress sutures define the antihelical fold, and says Merck stitch patients generally do not need a dressing.[1]

Fritsch, an earlier user, combined the method with the Furnas technique and later argued that lasting results required cutting the cartilage; Merck disputes this.[2] Other approaches include Stenstrom cartilage scoring and the Fritsch method, which combines minimally invasive suturing with scoring.[1]

Possible problems include pain, suture extrusion, infection, rare suture granuloma, slight postoperative bleeding and relapse, in which the ear protrudes again.[2] For otoplasty generally, Wikipedia lists suture extrusion behind the ear as the most common complication, with overcorrection and unnatural contours considered the most significant.[1]
No studies found on the Merck stitch itself. Studies of related closed otoplasty techniques exist, such as percutaneous adjustable closed otoplasty, but are separate procedures.

card.summary: A closed ear-pinning method using stitches through tiny stab incisions; documented but with little published outcome data.

quick.overview:
The Merck stitch is a closed ear-pinning technique placing sutures through small puncture incisions instead of an open posterior incision. It was published in 2013.

Sources describing it are sparse.
quick.mechanism: Sutures placed through stab incisions reshape the cartilage without cutting it.
quick.risks: General suture-otoplasty risks include suture extrusion, hematoma, infection and recurrence; no technique-specific studies were found.

chain: Sutures placed through small stab incisions behind the ear
Sutures draw the antihelix and ear closer to the head
Ears sit flatter and look more proportionate
angle.text: The stitches set prominent ears back toward the head without cutting cartilage or skin, so the ears look less protruding. Merck's method is described as suitable for all protruding ears in his experience.
